correspondence.component_scope: Northeastern Mifafí opening and southward El Águila–Apartaderos connector
correspondence.finding: Figure 7 maps the opening running northeast, turning south, receiving the separately shown El Águila and El Balcón branches, and continuing past Apartaderos. Figure 2 overlaps this headward setting. The p. 32 route description locates the source setting in the Sierra de La Culata, distinguishes the Mifafí cartographic name and identifies the El Águila junction before the Chama continuation. The selected beginning follows this mapped chain, not an adjacent eastern drainage. No exact local-name transition vertex is assigned.
correspondence.correspondence: Overlapping original-publication cartography and bounded supporting prose read at ordinary component/corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Southwest turn and upper Chama past Mucuchíes
correspondence.finding: Figure 7 follows the main route southwest from Apartaderos through the Mucuchíes vicinity and distinguishes La Toma, Mucuchache, Saisai, Gavidia and other side branches. Figure 2 overlaps the same upper corridor along the valley between the La Culata and Sierra Nevada mountain belts. The selected route remains on the receiving Chama trunk.
correspondence.correspondence: Overlapping original-publication cartography and bounded supporting prose read at ordinary component/corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Mérida–Ejido valley and major tributary junction settings
correspondence.finding: Figure 2 depicts the selected southwest-trending main valley through the Mérida–Ejido setting. It separately draws and labels Mucujún, Albarregas, La González and the southeastern Nuestra Señora/Tostós branch. These are lateral junction relationships; no uniform Chama name is assigned to those tributaries.
correspondence.correspondence: Overlapping original-publication cartography and bounded supporting prose read at ordinary component/corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower intramontane valley toward Estanques and Mocotíes
correspondence.finding: The regional map carries the Chama west/southwest past Lagunillas toward the bend below the San Pablo tributary setting. The selected corridor corresponds to the mapped Chama approach from the east; the long Mocotíes valley comes independently from the southwest. The chapter describes the opposed Chama and Mocotíes valley directions and their joining before the northward gorge.
correspondence.correspondence: Overlapping original-publication cartography and bounded supporting prose read at ordinary component/corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Mocotíes receiving junction, northward gorge and El Vigía transition
correspondence.finding: Figure 2 shows the southwest Mocotíes joining the selected eastern Chama approach and the receiving course turning north through a narrow mountain outlet to El Vigía. The prose independently describes the gorge after the junction and the exit to the lake depression. The selected line takes the northward receiver rather than following Mocotíes upstream. No intervening reservoir or lake passage is depicted.
correspondence.correspondence: Overlapping original-publication cartography and bounded supporting prose read at ordinary component/corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Chama lowland corridor north of El Vigía
correspondence.finding: Figure 2 continuously connects the El Vigía exit with the northward Chama lowland course toward southern Lago de Maracaibo. Supporting prose separates this lacustrine-plain setting from the intramontane basin and describes downstream anastomosing and meandering forms. The selected route follows this same general corridor; exact present-day lowland channel position is not established.
correspondence.correspondence: Overlapping original-publication cartography and bounded supporting prose read at ordinary component/corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual terminal into southern Lago de Maracaibo
correspondence.finding: Figure 2 visibly connects the mapped and labeled lower Río Chama to the southern lake shoreline, with the full upstream corridor still in view. The chapter describes a deltaic terminal and names Lago de Maracaibo as its receiving waterbody. This supports the selected terminal setting at ordinary corridor scale without equating the lake outlet with the open Caribbean coast or fixing an exact modern delta branch/mouth point.
correspondence.correspondence: Overlapping original-publication cartography and bounded supporting prose read at ordinary component/corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Northeastern selected opening and headward branch transfer
correspondence.finding: The selected opening lies northeast of the clearly traceable Cañazas trunk. The official 1:50,000 view stops short of that initial headward corridor. The independent 1:250,000 view shows additional northeastern branches, but does not unambiguously account for the entire selected opening and its choice of connection onto the trunk. The 1:160,000 basin original provides the surrounding Cañazas/Sábalo network, without resolving that opening-to-branch correspondence.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastern southward course, southern turn and west-northwest approach to the reservoir
correspondence.finding: Beyond the unresolved headward part, the readable mapping shows the Cañazas-side north-south course, an eastern Río Sábalo tributary, the large southern turn and the west-northwest course toward the eastern reservoir arm. MiAmbiente distinguishes this corridor from the northern upper-Bayano/Piriá drainage. IMHPA separately identifies Cañazas ante Embalse on this eastern river. These observations support the lower eastern corridor without extending its hydronym to every initial branch.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastern lake entry and connections with separately entering tributaries
correspondence.finding: The Cañazas-side corridor reaches the eastern impounded-water system. The basin original also shows the separately entering upper Bayano from the Piriá sector to the north, Río Tortí from the south and the adjacent Ipetí and Curtí arms. They are connections to the common reservoir, not evidence that all incoming rivers are named Bayano.

correspondence.component_scope: Central and northern reservoir passages, western reservoir and fragment transition
correspondence.finding: The original basin map and bounded official cartography show one connected, branching reservoir, with northern tributary arms, central narrows, peninsulas and islands, and the western lake body. Both selected fragments are accounted for in this generalized reservoir setting, including their retained transition in the western lake area. The source supports a connected impoundment passage, not a surveyed channel following the modeled line through the lake. Named off-selected tributaries and arms remain distinct.

correspondence.component_scope: Reservoir outlet, dam vicinity and western downstream river
correspondence.finding: The mapped western outlet connects the reservoir to the downstream Bayano corridor. ARAP identifies the lake as an impoundment of the Bayano for power generation, and IMHPA distinguishes Bayano Sitio de Presa from Lago Bayano. The selected route then follows the westward and southwestward river, with the Cañita-side connection and the Mamoní junction in the Chepo/Coquira sector identifiable in the basin original.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower river, selected ending and coastal continuation
correspondence.finding: The basin original labels the broad lower watercourse Río Bayano o Chepo and shows its connection past the La Coquera/Sabaneta sector toward the Pacific coast. The selected ending belongs to this lower estuarine corridor, rather than establishing an exact open-coast mouth. The neighboring Río Viejo/Río Chico and Chichebre-side network is separately depicted; those names are not transferred to the selected Bayano reach. The original source supplies the broad estuarine-water connection that the separate line-only drainage layers omit.

The selected beginning is the short northern-flowing feeder west of Timbaúba, through a small unnamed blue-mapped impoundment and the São Bento/Cachoeira-side approach. It joins the Bonsucesso corridor; the initial feeder is not automatically named Rio Jacu or Rio Bonsucesso.

The connected Rio Bonsucesso course passes the waterbody by Bonsucesso and the Rch. da Telha junction, then continues north through São Miguel and Algodão toward Bola/Bolas. Rch. de Santa Rita and Rch. dos Cavalos are separate side approaches. The larger Santa Rita-side reservoir is not the selected Bonsucesso passage.

The selected line follows the northern Bonsucesso approach by Trapiá, where the western Rio do Trapiá joins, then the Jacu/Boa Vista and Melo–Curral do Meio corridor. It continues through Mari and Passagem to the Campo Comprido meeting by Juçá, and northeast toward Cabaças. The western Campo Comprido/Boqueirão do Cais reservoir branch is distinguished from this selected southern approach; Rio Jacu, Rio Bonsucesso and Rio do Trapiá labels retain their bounded local scope.

The connected northern approach crosses the Picuí/Cerro Corá/Campestre sheet margins toward the Espinheiro and Rio Japi setting. The independent engineering plate identifies the later Retiro reservoir body, incoming arms and northeastern dam on this corridor. The selected natural continuation is the Japi-labelled river toward Japi town; the westward Retiro–Boqueirão do Cais adutora is a different, artificial connection. The2009 river originals establish the natural corridor before impoundment, the2019 original plate locates the reservoir/dam within it, and the2022 primary notice confirms the construction chronology. Current inundation extent is not claimed.

North/east of Japi and Boqueirão, the selected river proceeds through the Salgado/Serra Bonita and Jacó-side approach into Açude Público JapiII. The mapped reservoir body and its northern/northeastern outlet continue through Picos, Cruz São Pedro and Amarração toward São José do Campestre. This is a positively mapped reservoir connection; it is not inferred from the model alone.

At São José do Campestre and Barrinha the original directly labels Rio Jacu. The selected northern/western approach meets the distinct southern Pituaçu-side approach and continues through the bend toward Jacu/Poço Salgado and eastward along the Serrinha–Santo Antônio side. Nearby Trairi, Arapuá, Sombra Grande, Pituaçu, Barriguda and Cajazeiras waterbodies are not all assigned as selected passages.

The directly mapped Jacu corridor continues east along the Serrinha–Santo Antônio margin through the Redenção and Passagem setting. The northern Jacu-Mirim approach and southern Macacos/Santo Antônio approach meet the receiving system separately; their local tributary names are not extended over the selected group.

The selected course turns southeast from Passagem, is directly labelled Rio Jacu, receives the separate southward Jundiá-side tributary, and bends through the Espírito Santo setting before continuing northeast toward Goianinha. The municipal originals positively bridge this connector; the separate northern Riacho Fundo/Mosela waterbody corridor is not substituted for it.

The lower river enters the Goianinha–Arês channel/wetland setting and the southwestern arm of Lagoa Guaraíras near Umari de Baixo. The selected rendered terminal lies in that receiving lagoon setting. The lagoon has a mapped Atlantic inlet by Tibau do Sul farther downstream; the selected endpoint is not treated as a surveyed ocean mouth. Papary, Papeba, Baldum and Arari are distinct northern approaches, not selected passages. Regional and municipal cartography establish the lagoon-scale correspondence without demanding exact agreement with each estuarine channel or bank.
The initial channel identity, dry or wet condition, and links through the headward agricultural/managed-water landscape have not been established by original cartography.
